speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The amendments proposed in the Bill arose from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority's (ACRA's) regular review of its regulatory functions to foster a trusted and vibrant business environment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first set of amendments strengthen safeguards against the misuse of companies for unlawful purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Companies Act 1967, the Registrar of Companies may refuse registration of a company if it is likely to be used for an unlawful purpose or for purposes prejudicial to public peace, welfare or good order in Singapore; or if its registration contravenes national security or interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will refer to these conditions as "grounds for refusal" for short.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the law currently does not explicitly require the courts or the Registrar to deny applications for restoration of struck-off companies, foreign companies or limited liability partnerships based on the grounds for refusal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This aligns with the existing criteria for refusing company registrations under the Companies Act 1967, and for winding up a company under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The second set of key amendments are aimed at safeguarding shareholders' interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, a company may purchase its own shares through a selective off-market purchase, conducted outside of a securities exchange or not under an equal access scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This requires approval by a special resolution, with at least 75% of voting rights in favour, excluding the votes of the shareholders whose shares are being acquired.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, in situations where a company has different classes of shares, this process may not sufficiently account for the interests of shareholders in the affected class who are not part of the selective off-market purchase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Tier 1 which is an existing provision in section 76D of the Companies Act 1967, requires the approval by all shareholders, regardless of class of shares, excluding the shareholders whose shares are being acquired.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Tier 2, which is newly introduced under this Bill, requires the consent by the relevant shareholders within the affected class of shares, but excluding the shareholders whose shares are being acquired.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This allows for shareholders within the affected class of shares to have a larger say in approving the selective off-market purchase.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To simplify implementation for the new Tier 2 approval, companies can obtain written consent from affected shareholders, and do not need to convene a separate class meeting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The third set of amendments strengthen the regulatory framework for companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Section 157 of the Companies Act 1967 requires a director to manage the company and act in its best interests, honestly and with reasonable diligence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A breach of the provision is an offence, and currently the penalty is a fine not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, when compared to penalties for equivalent offences in other leading common law jurisdictions, we found that there was scope for an upward revision of the penalties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This provides stronger penalties to deter potential offenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The fourth set of key amendments reduce the regulatory burden on companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Since inception of the Companies Act in 1967, a company's registered office must be open to the public for at least three hours each business day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was primarily intended to facilitate access to company records by any persons entitled to inspect them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To reduce the regulatory burden on companies while maintaining the rights of those who need access to company records in the company's registered office, clauses 52, 89, 90, 99 of the Bill abolish the minimum opening hours requirement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Instead, the Bill provides that persons entitled to inspect any company record must give the company reasonable notice of their intent to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Upon being given such notice, companies must then make such records available for inspection for at least two hours during each of the relevant business days.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will give companies more flexibility to determine the operating hours of their registered offices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For avoidance of doubt, the proposed amendment will not affect service of documents at the company's registered office.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Companies Act 1967 allows a document to be served on a company by leaving it at or sending it by registered post to the registered office of the company, without requiring the registered office to be physically open.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The final set of amendments are intended to enhance the regulatory regime of public accountants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Currently, audit reports are usually signed off by accounting entities, rather than the specific individual public accountant who performed the audit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The identity of the public accountant primarily responsible for the audit engagement is not disclosed in the audit report itself, though this information is available in the register of auditors on ACRA's Bizfile.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I rise in support of the Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Bill 2025.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill represents another important step to keep Singapore’s corporate and accounting frameworks progressive, trusted and competitive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It modernises key provisions in the Companies Act and Accountants Act.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It strengthens governance, enhances transparency and ensures our laws continue to support enterprise growth and innovation in a fast-changing business environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill removes outdated rules, such as the statement in lieu of prospectus and the old requirement for offices to stay open three hours a day for public inspection.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Replacing that with a flexible two-hour access window, subject to reasonable notice, is a sensible update that reflects today's digital practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also welcome the potential exemption from full Singapore Financial Reporting Standards for smaller entities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If applied with clear criteria, this can make accounting simpler and more cost-effective for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), while preserving transparency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taken together, these are forward-looking moves that make compliance easier, reduce friction for businesses and strengthen Singapore’s standing as a trusted and efficient business hub.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Mr Speaker, I would like to highlight several practical concerns from the perspective of SMEs, which make up the vast majority of registered companies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It removes the right to inspect physical documents but retains the right for anyone to obtain an electronic copy or extract from ACRA.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some shareholder details, such as names, shareholdings and addresses, are already available in the ACRA Biz Profile.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, this change expands both the mode and depth of access.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This electronic register contains more detailed information, including share transfer dates, ownership history, and in some cases, residential addresses where no business address is listed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By allowing anyone to easily obtain these details through ACRA, the Bill could increase the exposure of personal and commercial data.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For small family firms and investment holding companies, this raises legitimate concerns about privacy, confidentiality and data protection.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Disclosures required under the Companies Act are exempt from the PDPA’s consent rules.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, while this legal alignment is clear, the policy implications merit attention.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the electronic register becomes more accessible, ACRA should continue to apply data protection principles in practice, such as masking residential addresses, limit access to essential information and ensuring robust safeguards against misuse or data scraping.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A privacy-by-design approach will preserve transparency while protecting the trust and personal data of business owners.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I therefore urge the Ministry to work with ACRA to implement appropriate redaction and access safeguards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, masking residential addresses, or limiting sensitive information to request-based access rather than automatic downloads.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, the Bill introduces stricter report and notification requirements, coupled with higher penalties.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Companies must now report disqualifications or changes in key appointments promptly and accurately.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, smaller firms without compliance staff may find it challenging to keep pace with the new requirements.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A single delay, even if unintentional, could result in penalties that feel disproportionate to their scale or intent.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Without clearer thresholds or guidance, SMEs may be unsure whether they qualify or how they apply for such exemptions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This uncertainty could lead to confusion and inconsistent compliance when the changes come into force.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, for the members' Register, apply proportionate safeguards, such as masking residential addresses or limiting sensitive data to request-based access.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This preserves transparency while reducing the risk of misuse.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ACRA could also publish clear, plain English compliance guides, with templates, calendars and examples of "reasonable notice" for record inspections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, if the intent is to ease compliance for smaller firms, publish the qualifying thresholds, such as revenue size or asset size, well in advance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Complement this with outreach through SME Centres and professional bodies, so businesses can prepare their systems ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, this Bill strengthens Singapore's reputation as a place where governance is strong, business is trusted, and laws are modern and fair.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It strikes a balance between transparency and privacy, between accountability and practicality.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we refine our laws, it is worthy to note that smaller enterprises form the backbone of our economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When rules are clear, proportionate and supported by guidance, they do more than ensure compliance.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They are our innovators, job creators and community builders.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But even as we pursue higher standards, we must ensure that our SMEs, which form the heartbeat of our business ecosystem, are able to comply effectively and affordably.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many SMEs in Singapore are lean operations often family-run, entrepreneur-driven, with small teams juggling multiple roles.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While stronger reporting and record-keeping can improve transparency, they can also raise compliance costs, especially for smaller firms with limited resources.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If compliance becomes too complex or expensive, we risk discouraging innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Funds that could go into hiring, product development or market expansion may, instead, be channelled into paperwork, audits and consultancy fees.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We must, therefore, ensure that transparency and efficiency progress hand-in-hand, especially for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Good governance enhances credibility and access to capital.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, if SMEs find the new requirements difficult to fulfil, they may appear riskier to lenders or investors, ironically, reducing their access to financing or grants.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In an economy where many SMEs depend on trade finance, venture capital and Government grants, the risk is real to them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That said, Mr Speaker, this Bill also presents great opportunities for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enhanced corporate governance and ownership transparency will build investor confidence, attract long-term capital and reinforce Singapore's standing as a trusted and competitive global business hub.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Done right, this Bill will not only uphold our clean and credible reputation, it will also empower SMEs to grow on a stronger and more sustainable foundation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The key lies in implementation, ensuring proportionality, support and flexibility.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I had the privilege of engaging in a dialogue with a group of predominantly Chinese-speaking SME owners at the Society of Modern Management Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They shared valuable insights about their experiences and challenges in doing business locally and they offered many constructive views.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They expressed confidence in the future and strong support for our national policies.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, they thanked the Government for its long-lasting commitment to supporting SMEs through various policies and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This consistent policy support has given SMEs a strong foundation to navigate in this increasingly complex global environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Thus, allow me to offer five practical recommendations to make the implementation more SME-friendly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Adjust requirements based on company size, revenue or staff strength.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Larger firms can meet full reporting standards, while micro and small enterprises should simplify templates that maintain accountability without excessive cost.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enhance ACRA's Bizfile+ platform with easy-to-use templates and automation tools.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Where possible, integrate SMEs' accounting software directly with ACRA systems to reduce manual data entry and errors.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Provide training, webinars and advisory hotlines to help SMEs comply efficiently.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Equip local accounting firms and trade associations to mentor and guide smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, SMEs are important backbone of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They make up over 99% of all businesses, contribute nearly half of our GDP and employ about 70% of our workers.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The growth and vitality of SMEs directly affect the robustness and resilience of our economy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It can be said that when SMEs do well, Singapore does well.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I had the privilege of engaging in a dialogue with a group of predominantly Chinese speaking SMEs owner at The Society of Modern Management Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They shared valuable insights about their experiences and challenges in doing business locally and offered many constructive views.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This exchange made me feel deeply that the entrepreneurship, flexible thinking and unwavering determination of our entrepreneurs are important driving forces behind Singapore’s continuous economic transformation and growth.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They expressed confidence in the future and strong support for our national policies.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, they also thanked the Government's long-standing commitment to support SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Through various initiatives, such as the Enterprise Transformation Programme, the Government has actively promoted digitalisation, innovation and internationalisation, providing valuable resources and direction for businesses.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Corporate and Accounting Laws (Amendment) Bill 2025 further demonstrates the Government's continued commitment to improving the business environment and enhancing governance standards.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These measures will not only enhance Singapore's international reputation, but also consolidate our position as a business hub that is trustworthy, stable and reliable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Corporate transparency is essential to preserve trust in our markets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, we must also protect the agility and entrepreneurial spirit that define Singapore's SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Let us pass legislation through strengthened accountability without stifling ambition and empower our SMEs to grow, innovate and continue contributing to Singapore's prosperity for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have spoken on two main themes relating to compliance costs for companies and the importance of data protection, and I will address these in turn.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Finance and ACRA regularly review the corporate regulatory framework to reduce compliance costs for companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By removing the requirement, we are giving companies more flexibility in managing their operations and reduce unnecessary staffing costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, some companies can cease engaging corporate secretarial services, if they were engaged solely to meet the minimum operating hours requirements, even when their business operations do not actually require the registered office to be open.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Most of the amendments relating to strengthening the regulatory framework for companies are existing obligations under the Companies Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Companies are already required to file their annual returns and maintain proper accounting records.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Edward Chia mentioned that the Bill introduces stricter reporting and notification requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The "new" reporting requirement Mr Chia mentioned relates to the amended section 173A of the Companies Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Currently, section 173A requires companies to report changes in position-holder details within 14 days.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, I emphasise that companies only need to report a director's disqualification after becoming aware of the director's disqualification and companies have 14 days to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Both Mr Edward Chia and Mr Lee Hong Chuang asked if financial reporting and auditing requirements could be simplified for SMEs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current regulatory framework already provides for this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, small companies can prepare their financial statements using a simplified financial reporting framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Companies Act also exempts companies from audit requirements if their revenue, assets and/or employees are below certain thresholds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will continue to review these compliance requirements to see if more companies can benefit from these simplified frameworks or exemptions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA is also studying how to make digital filing for financial statements simpler.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will give companies and individuals time to prepare.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, when ACRA enforces these requirements, it will do so in a measured manner and ensure that any sanction is proportionate to the circumstances of the breach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, let me address Mr Chia's questions on data protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He asked whether replacing the right to inspect the Registrar's physical documents with electronic access would change the scope of personal and company data exposed to the public.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, members of the public can already inspect a private company's electronic register of members upon payment of the prescribed fees under section 12(2)(d) of the Companies Act 1967.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amendments simply update the mode of access by replacing physical inspection with electronic access to the same information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This removes an obsolete requirement without prejudicing or expanding rights.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In relation to privacy and data protection concerns raised by Mr Chia, ACRA is mindful of the need to balance corporate transparency with personal data protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, ACRA implemented the filing of a contact address last year to enhance personal data protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the Registrar will make public the contact address and not the residential address, I encourage shareholders and position holders to file a non-residential contact address to better protect their personal data.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, ACRA needs to know the residential address, that is for ACRA's purposes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But sometimes when you need to have personal service of court documents, for example, you can put a contact address which the documents can be served, and that is what is made publicly available.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Chia, Mr Lee, any clarifications for Minister?
